understand:
Roommates splitting groceries, electricity and Wi-Fi — the real need is trust: everyone wants to see that the maths is fair without doing it themselves. So the core loop is log an expense → see balances → settle up.

A true shared ledger needs accounts and a backend so every phone sees the same data. For an on-device prototype I'll keep one ledger per phone and say so in the scope note. Decisions worth asking: equal vs custom splits, pairwise vs simplified debts, and what happens when someone moves out. Several entities plus an algorithm make this intermediate.
plan:
Three entities: Member, Expense (paidBy + splitBetween by member id) and Settlement. Money must be integer paise — floats would make balances drift by a paisa.

Four screens share the same data, so Context + useReducer beats prop drilling, and a reducer gives every change a name. Balances should be derived with useMemo, never stored. The algorithm goes in pure functions first: net balances, then greedy matching of the largest debtor and creditor (at most n − 1 payments). Build order: tokens and money maths → algorithm → context → components → screens → App.js.
build: Starting with money.js: parseAmount, formatMoney with Indian grouping, and splitEvenly that hands leftover paise to the first people so shares always sum to the total. balances.js stays pure so it's easy to test. In the provider, the save effect must wait for the first load. The form derives its errors from state and only shows them after a save attempt.
explain: For an intermediate learner, the key story is the unidirectional loop: screen → action creator → reducer → new state → derived balances → re-render. I'll trace adding an expense through all of it, and spend extra time on why paise are integers and how the greedy algorithm terminates.
learn: The concepts that make this app work: data modelling, pure functions, array methods, useReducer, immutability, context, useMemo, form validation and AsyncStorage. The quiz should test the why — integer money, exact splits, new references, derived data and the n − 1 bound. Challenges escalate from a monthly total to editing to unequal splits.
